pattern BITSAT (2022 onward) - 130 questions (custom): 15 questions; profile balanced; difficulty match; seed 11
resuming: 4 verified question(s) kept, 11 to generate

Physics: All three keys check out (v = √(rg tanθ) = 30 m s⁻¹ = 108 km h⁻¹; F ∝ I₁I₂/d gives 4×10⁻⁵ N m⁻¹; the null point lies 20 cm beyond B), and the spread across mechanics, magnetism and electrostatics is sensible with no overlapping concepts. The level is on the easy side, however: Q1 and Q2 are single-formula substitutions solvable in well under a minute, so at least one item should demand two or three linked steps to match BITSAT's typical demand for speed with some reasoning. Only a small wording fix in Q2 is needed before printing.

[minor] The phrase "the separation between the wires is made three times" is unidiomatic and leaves the multiplier's reference implicit; reword as "the separation is tripled" (or "made three times its original value").

Chemistry: All three keys check out (0.2 mol Al → 26.7 g AlCl3; Statement II fails because of the d-block contraction giving Ga < Al; the drawn isomer is (2S,3R) so its enantiomer is (2R,3S) with 4 stereoisomers), and the topics — mole concept, periodicity, stereochemistry — are distinct with no overlap. The level runs from very easy (q4) to the upper end of the 90-second budget (q6, which needs two Fischer R/S assignments plus an isomer count), so the section is slightly top-heavy in difficulty spread but acceptable. Only cosmetic fixes (broken LaTeX in q4, redundant figure text in q6) are needed before printing.
[minor] The balanced equation is corrupted by lost LaTeX escapes (it prints as "2 ext{Al} + 3 ext{Cl}_2 ightarrow 2 ext{AlCl}_3"), so \text and \rightarrow must be restored before printing.

[minor] The stem verbally reproduces the whole Fischer projection that the figure already shows ("Reading from top to bottom, it is: ..."), which is redundant and awkwardly phrased; trim it to a single reference to the figure.

English Proficiency: The three items are keyed correctly and the distractors are cleanly non-defensible: Q7's contrastive "but" forces "hollowness", and the two comprehension items test genuinely different skills (global main idea versus the purpose of a specific analogy) on a well-constructed, appropriately sized passage. Level and length are suitable for BITSAT, though the vocabulary item is on the easier side and the section as shown lacks the usual spread of grammar/synonym-antonym/rearrangement types. Only a small grammatical correction inside the passage is needed before printing.

[minor] In the passage, "inevitably distorts either area, shape, or distance" uses the two-term correlative "either...or" with three items; change to "distorts area, shape, or distance" (or "at least one of area, shape, or distance"), since faulty grammar is unacceptable in an English Proficiency passage.

Logical Reasoning: All three keys are correct and the wording and option sets are clean, with plausible near-miss distractors in the two coding items. However, the section is unbalanced: two of the three questions rely on the identical constant-shift alphabet mechanic, and the syllogism is a textbook two-premise chain, so the overall difficulty sits below the BITSAT norm. Replace one coding item with a different reasoning type (e.g., blood relations, seating arrangement or number series) and raise the syllogism to a three-premise or possibility-based form.

[major] This letter-analogy is solved by exactly the same uniform alphabet-shift rule as Q10 (+3 here versus +2 there), so the two items test essentially the same skill and one must be replaced with a different reasoning type.

Mathematics: All three items are mathematically sound: the integrand in Q13 reduces to e^x(csc²x − cot x) giving −e^x cot x, the focal-chord relation 1/l₁ + 1/l₂ = 1/a yields 1/3 for y² = 12x, and 36 has nine divisors so 2⁹ = 512 subsets, matching the stated keys. The spread across integral calculus, conics and sets is reasonable and each is solvable well within 90 seconds, with Q13 the only one demanding real manipulation. Q15 is at the easy end (divisor count plus power of two) but still acceptable as a quick-scoring item; consider adding one moderate-difficulty item elsewhere in the section to balance the overall level.
